unit.can_do_en: plan a walk in the forest and talk about berries.

brief.situation_en: Aino and Maria in the forest.

judge.reason: Kato/katso is only a register difference; same meaning.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Are we allowed to pick them?

judge.reason: Saaks/saako and poimii/poimia are colloquial forms; same question.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.gloss_en: Yes. Finland has everyone's right to roam.

judge.reason: Suomes/Suomessa is a dropped ending; same statement.
Tarkottaa/tarkoittaa is a spelling variant; same question.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.text_puhe: Kaikki saa liikkuu luonnos ja poimii marjoja.
lines.text_kirja: Kaikki saavat liikkua luonnossa ja poimia marjoja.
lines.gloss_en: Everyone can move around in nature and pick berries.

judge.reason: Colloquial singular agreement (saa) and dropped endings; same meaning.

puhe.text: Kaikki saa liikkuu luonnos ja poimii marjoja.

kirja.text: Kaikki saavat liikkua luonnossa ja poimia marjoja.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.text_puhe: Niitäkin, mut ole varovainen. Osa on myrkyllisiä.
lines.text_kirja: Niitäkin, mutta ole varovainen. Osa on myrkyllisiä.
lines.gloss_en: Those too, but be careful. Some are poisonous.

judge.reason: Mut/mutta is a register difference; the rest is identical.

puhe.text: Niitäkin, mut ole varovainen. Osa on myrkyllisiä.

kirja.text: Niitäkin, mutta ole varovainen. Osa on myrkyllisiä.

judge.reason: Mä/minä and vaan/vain are register differences; same meaning.

forms.why_en: This is how you tell someone to look: katso. Speech drops the s: kato.
Plural 'some' takes -ita: mustikka becomes mustikoita, kk turning into k.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.lemma_meaning_en: to get, to be allowed to
forms.why_en: Saada, may, with the question ending -ko: saako? Speech uses -ks: saaks.
The partitive plural of ne 'they': niitä, used after kokeilla 'to try'.
This is the dictionary form, used after saa, 'may'. Speech turns the ending -ia into -ii: poimii.

forms.lemma_meaning_en: to get, to be allowed to
forms.why_en: From saada. Mitä saa olla? is a set phrase for 'What can I get you?'
Adds -ssa for 'in', and si changes to e: Suomi becomes Suomessa. Speech shortens -ssa to -s: Suomessa becomes Suomes.
The form of olla, to be, for he, she or it. People say it the same way.
Finns say this with -t, as several rights: jokamiehenoikeus becomes jokamiehenoikeudet.
The partitive of mikä, what. Mitä saa olla? means What can I get you?
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Tarkoittaa, to mean. With 'tuo sana' the verb ends in a long vowel. Speech drops the i: tarkottaa.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.

forms.lemma_meaning_en: to get, to be allowed to
forms.why_en: Books add -vat for 'they': saavat. Speech uses the short form saa with kaikki, 'everyone'.
This is the dictionary form, used after saa, 'may'. Speech turns the ending -ua into -uu.
Adds -ssa for 'in': luonto becomes luonnossa, nt turning into nn. Speech says luonnos.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Plural 'some' takes -ja: marja becomes marjoja, the last a turning into o.
Mahtava, great. Said alone about good news it ends in -aa: Mahtavaa!
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Adds -t for more than one: sieni becomes sienet.
Niitä means 'them'. The ending -kin adds 'too': niitäkin.
Speech shortens mutta to mut. Books write mutta.
The imperative for one person is olla without its ending: ole. 'Ole hyvä' means 'here you are' or 'you're welcome'.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Plural 'some' takes -iä: myrkyllinen becomes myrkyllisiä.
Speech shortens minä to mä. Books write minä.
Poimia means to pick. The ending -n goes with minä: poimin.
Speech says vaan. Books write vain.
